name: Talmud
info: The Talmud is the central text of Rabbinic Judaism after the Hebrew Bible: the Mishnah and the Gemara's commentary on it, compiled in Galilee and Babylonia between the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE and the early seventh century.

facts.made: The rabbis of the Land of Israel and Babylonia: the Tannaim, who produced the Mishnah in the second century CE, and the Amoraim of the third to fifth centuries, with later editors called Savoraim; tradition names Rav Ashi and Ravina II as compilers of the Babylonian Talmud
facts.form: A commentary of 63 tractates in six orders, written largely in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic with Mishnaic and Biblical Hebrew quotations; the Babylonian Talmud has about 2.5 million words and the Vilna edition 2,711 folio pages
facts.where: The only complete manuscript, Munich Codex Hebraica 95 (1342); Cairo Genizah fragments; the Oxford, Firenze and Vatican codices; copies in study houses worldwide
facts.known: The Mishnah and Gemara together; the back and forth of rabbinic debate; the Oral Torah as Jewish tradition holds it; law (halakha) alongside legend (aggadah); the Vilna page with Rashi and Tosafot; a long history of commentary; the Disputation of Paris and the burnings of its copies

t: The Talmud is the Mishnah together with the Gemara, the rabbinic commentary on it; the Babylonian Talmud is the one usually meant, and in Rabbinic Judaism it ranks second in authority only to the Hebrew Bible.
It records the disagreements of thousands of rabbis rather than only their conclusions, and it mixes law with legend, ethics, history and folklore.
Its history outside Judaism includes disputations, censorship and burnings of its copies, and also close study by Christian scholars and a printing at Venice that became the model for later editions.
dyk: Because the Talmud's page was set in print by Daniel Bomberg in Venice between 1520 and 1523, almost every printing since has followed the same pagination, and a reader today still cites a passage by its folio, such as Berachot 23b.
ev: The destruction of the Second Temple, from which Talmudic tradition is dated as emerging
The Tannaim produce the Mishnah, the framework on which the Talmud is built
The Jerusalem Talmud is compiled in Galilee
Ravina II, by medieval chronicles' reckoning, dies, and the Talmud is said to have stopped
Modern scholars think the Babylonian Talmud was most likely completed, after a last redaction by the Savoraim
The Disputation of Paris examines charges against the Talmud brought by Nicholas Donin
Daniel Bomberg begins printing the first complete Babylonian Talmud at Venice
Menachem Romm of Vilna prints the edition on which most later ones are modelled

sections.origins:
The Talmud is a central text of Rabbinic Judaism and a primary source of Jewish law (halakha) and theology. Talmudic tradition emerged and was compiled between the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE and the Arab conquest in the early seventh century. It rests on the Oral Torah, which Orthodox Judaism maintains was revealed in some form together with the written Torah.

Its first layer is the Mishnah, a compilation of legal opinions and debates by the rabbis known as the Tannaim, teachers of the second century CE. The rabbis of the third to fifth centuries, the Amoraim, then produced the two Talmuds by analysing and debating the Mishnah. In antiquity there were two major centres of such scholarship, the academies of Syria Palaestina and of Babylonia, and a Talmud was compiled in each. Among the Babylonian academies were Nehardea, Nisibis, Mahoza, Pumbedita and Sura. The Amoraim began to use Aramaic, then the spoken vernacular, in their discussions around the year 200. Recent scholarship has argued at length that the Babylonian Talmud is also a product of Sasanian culture, drawing on Greek-Roman, Middle Persian and Syriac sources, and that its contents likely trace to that setting whatever the date of its final redaction.
sections.content:
The Talmud follows the structure of the Mishnah. It is divided into six orders, known as Shisha Sedarim or by the abbreviation Shas, and these into 63 tractates (masekhtot), each on a more focused subject, with 517 chapters in all. Not every tractate has a Gemara, and the Babylonian commentary covers 37 of the Mishnah's 63.

The Gemara is broadly a commentary on the Mishnah, arising from a long practice of rabbis analysing and debating it, called shakla v'tarya, 'taking and throwing'. Each discussion is an edited passage called a sugya, often framed as an exchange between a questioner (makshan) and an answerer (tartzan). Much of it is legal, and it seeks the biblical basis for a Mishnaic rule and the reasoning that links the two. It also holds narratives, sermons and sayings, called aggadah, which make up about a third of the Babylonian Talmud and a sixth of the Jerusalem. It cites baraitot, teachings of the Oral Torah that did not enter the Mishnah, and it records opinions that were not edited out. The work is largely in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic, with quotations of the Mishnah, baraitot and Tanakh in Hebrew.
sections.making:
Tradition holds that the foundations of the Babylonian analysis were laid by Abba Arika (175 to 247), a disciple of Judah ha-Nasi, and ascribes the compilation to two sages, Rav Ashi, president of the Sura Academy from 375 to 427, and Ravina II. The latest date traditionally given is 475, the year Ravina II died. Medieval sources vary: several chronicles put his death in 500 CE, Abraham ibn Daud gives 510, and Joseph ibn Tzaddik 505.

Even those who hold traditional views accept that the Savoraim made a final redaction in the sixth century. Historians have proposed a wide range of dates but think it most likely finished in the sixth century, or before the Muslim conquests of the mid-seventh at the latest, since it lacks Arabic loanwords and syntax. It must post-date the early fifth century, as it relies on the Jerusalem Talmud, which was compiled in Galilee, probably between the late fourth century and the first half of the fifth.

Modern scholars such as David Weiss Halivni and Shamma Friedman separate the Amoraic statements, usually brief, from the longer dialectic of the later Stammaitic authors. Rabbinic tradition holds that the sages cited in the Talmuds did not themselves write it, and that their teachings were edited into rough form around 450 CE (Yerushalmi) and 550 CE (Bavli).
sections.reception:
From its completion the Talmud became integral to Jewish scholarship, and a maxim in Pirkei Avot advocates its study from the age of 15. Adin Steinsaltz writes that no other work has had a comparable influence on the theory and practice of Jewish life. Until the Haskalah of the 18th and 19th centuries it was the centrepiece of Jewish culture in nearly all communities. Medieval commentary included the surviving full commentary of Chananel ben Chushiel, Rashi's classic commentary, and the Tosafot, collected by Ashkenazi rabbis to explain contradictory statements. Isaac Alfasi (1013 to 1103) extracted binding legal rulings. In the 15th and 16th centuries the intensive method of pilpul arose, and rabbis such as Judah Loew ben Bezalel criticised it. In the late 19th century Hayyim Soloveitchik developed the Brisker method.

Outside Judaism the response was divided. The Disputation of Paris of 1240 followed charges made by Nicholas Donin, a convert to Christianity, to Pope Gregory IX, and led to the first burning of copies in Paris in 1242. A Latin translation of 1,922 passages, the Extractiones de Talmud, was made in 1244 and 1245. Some Christian scholars, among them Johann Reuchlin and Johannes Buxtorf, studied it sympathetically.
sections.survival:
The only complete manuscript is Munich Codex Hebraica 95, from 1342. The earliest fragments, from the Cairo Genizah, date from the late seventh or eighth century. Ms. Oxford 2673 (1123) is the earliest Talmudic manuscript with a precisely known date, and Ms. Firenze 7 (1177) the earliest such with complete tractates.

Copies were burned and censored. After Donin's charges, copies were condemned and burned in Paris in 1242. A commission of Dominicans at Barcelona ordered passages cancelled in 1264. In Rome copies confiscated by the Inquisition were burned in the Campo de' Fiori on 9 September 1553, and a papal bull of 1554 introduced censorship. In 1564 Pius IV lifted the prohibition but required censorship, and the work could not be titled Talmud, hence the name Shas. The Basel edition of 1578 to 1581 omitted tractate Avodah Zarah. The omitted passages were kept in printed lists of errata, the Chesronos Hashas, and many were later recovered from uncensored manuscripts in the Vatican Library.

Soncino printed the first tractates in 1483. Daniel Bomberg printed the first complete edition at Venice from 1520 to 1523, thought relatively free of censorship, and the Vilna edition of the 1830s onward is now by far the most common. Scholars regard its text as not uniformly reliable, and there is no modern critical edition of the whole.
sections.legacy:
The Vilna Talmud, in 25 volumes, remains the basic text of Torah study in yeshivas and for scholars of Judaism, and its folio pagination is the convention of reference. Study methods keep changing: the Brisker method, now used in most yeshivas in some form, is sometimes criticised as a modern pilpul, and academic scholarship separates the text's strata and compares it with Zoroastrian texts to place it in its Iranian context, as Yaakov Elman and Shai Secunda do.

Translation has widened the audience. Adin Steinsaltz's modern Hebrew translation, begun in 1969 and finished in 2010, was followed by the Koren English edition in 42 volumes, the Schottenstein edition in 73 volumes completed in 2004, and Isidore Epstein's Soncino translation of 1935 to 1948. The William Davidson Talmud went online at Sefaria in 2017 under a Creative Commons licence. A Talmud for survivors of the Holocaust was printed in the US zone of Germany from 1947 to 1950.

The Talmud has also been attacked, often by antisemitic writers, such as August Rohling in 1871. Scholars point out that many of the criticisms rest on falsehoods or on quotations taken out of context, and the Anti-Defamation League has described fabricated passages. In South Korea, books titled Talmud, based on the writings of Marvin Tokayer rather than on the original, are widely read.

summary: The Talmud is the Mishnah with the Gemara's commentary on it, compiled by rabbis in Galilee and Babylonia between 70 CE and the early seventh century. The Babylonian Talmud is the one usually meant, and in Rabbinic Judaism it is second in authority only to the Hebrew Bible.

notes: start 200 is an editorial choice: the article gives no single start; it says tradition emerged after 70 CE, the Amoraim adopted Aramaic around 200, and the Babylonian Talmud consists of documents from the 3rd to 6th centuries.

The article contradicts itself on the Bomberg date (1520 to 1523 in the Editions section, 1520 in the Renaissance section, 1523 for the Jerusalem Talmud) and on the Slavita edition (heading 1795, text 1817). The Vilna edition is dated 1835 in its heading but 'first printed in the 1870s and 1880s' in its text; I wrote 'of the 1830s onward' in survival and 1835 in an event, which follows the heading and the Romm sentence under Slavita.

Dating of the compilation is given by the article as tradition c. 500 CE, with 'more likely the middle of the sixth century'; it also says Ravina II's death 811 SE = 500 CE, but Ravina's date in the 'Babylonian Talmud' section is 475. Both are attributed.
The article says Rav Ashi's presidency 375 to 427 and gives Ravina II's death as 475 (traditional); this is a gap I did not try to reconcile.

Left out: the Iran vice-president's 2012 claim, the Arabic translation controversy, the Christian and Muslim criticisms by named individuals, Candace Owens, because the article's coverage is thin or political; the first-century dating of the Wikkuah's '1,500 years old'.
The 'dyk' and the 1835 event rest on the article's statement that nearly all printings follow Bomberg's pagination.
